questions.q: What is prompting, in the framing used in this lesson?
options: Retraining the model's weights on your own data
Choosing the starting tokens so the next-token distribution is the one you want
Compressing the model so it runs faster
Writing SQL queries that the model executes
questions.explain: The model only predicts the next token given the text so far, so the prompt conditions that distribution. No weights change.

questions.q: Which set lists the four parts of a well-formed prompt described in this lesson?
options: Loss, optimizer, learning rate, epochs
Tokenizer, embedding, attention, softmax
Role or context, task, input data, output format
Train, validation, test, deployment
questions.explain: Role/context, a clear task, the input data kept separate from instructions, and the exact output format.

questions.q: Why does the few-shot ticket-labeling prompt end with the text "Label:"?
options: So the most likely next token is the label itself, in the format the examples showed
Because the API requires every prompt to end with a colon
To reset the temperature to zero
To tell the model to stop generating immediately
questions.explain: Ending on "Label:" after worked examples makes the label the natural continuation, in the exact shape of the examples.

questions.q: In the numpy demo, what happens to the probabilities as temperature drops from 1.0 to 0.2?
options: They become more uniform across all tokens
They stay identical because temperature only affects speed
The distribution concentrates on the highest-scoring token, giving near-deterministic output
The lowest-scoring token becomes the most likely
questions.explain: Dividing logits by a small T sharpens the softmax: the top token went from about 0.66 to about 0.99 in the demo.

questions.q: Which is the best way to know whether a change to a prompt actually improved it?
options: Read one or two outputs and go with your impression
Make the prompt longer, since longer always helps
Raise the temperature until the answers look more varied
Score both versions on a small labeled set, as you would evaluate a classifier
questions.explain: Treat prompts as code: version them and measure changes on labeled data instead of judging by a few samples.
